topics.description: A temporary effort with a defined start, end, and objective — distinct from ongoing operations.
Scope, time and cost, bounding quality. Changing one forces a change in another; pretending otherwise is how projects fail.
Anyone affected by or able to affect the project, whose expectations must be actively managed.
A tangible output, and a significant checkpoint in the schedule.
The phases from requirements through design, implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance.
Sequential phases, each completed before the next. Predictable when requirements are genuinely stable, brittle when they are not.
Iterative delivery in short cycles with continuous feedback, valuing responsiveness to change over following a fixed plan.
topics.notes: A named comparison and reliably examined.

topics.description: An agile framework built on fixed-length sprints, a prioritised backlog, and defined roles and ceremonies.
A fixed-length iteration, commonly two weeks, producing a potentially shippable increment.
Product owner owns priority, scrum master owns the process and removes impediments, and the development team owns delivery.
Sprint planning, daily standup, review and retrospective — the retrospective being where the process itself improves.
The ordered list of everything wanted, and the subset committed to the current sprint.
Continuous flow visualised on a board with work-in-progress limits, rather than fixed iterations.
A short statement of need from the user’s perspective, in the form as a role, I want a capability, so that a benefit.
The conditions that must hold for work to be considered complete, agreed before work starts.
The team-wide standard every item must meet — tested, reviewed, documented — as distinct from criteria specific to one story.
The smallest release that delivers real value and produces learning.
Sizing work relatively, and measuring how much a team completes per sprint to forecast. Velocity is a planning aid, not a productivity score.
A bar chart of tasks against time showing durations and dependencies, associated with plan-driven approaches.
The longest chain of dependent tasks, which determines the earliest possible finish. Delay here delays everything.
Identifying risks, assessing likelihood and impact, and planning responses before they materialise.
Uncontrolled growth of scope without matching adjustment to time or cost — the most common project failure mode.
The formal process by which scope changes are proposed, assessed and approved.
Clarifying who is responsible, accountable, consulted and informed for each activity.
Recording work and defects in a shared system so status is visible without asking.
Clients request, servers respond — the basic shape of nearly all networked applications.
Presentation, application logic, and data tiers separated so each can be scaled and changed independently.
topics.notes: Identifying which tier a component belongs to is a likely question.

topics.description: One deployable unit containing the whole application. Simple to run, harder to scale or change in parts.
Independently deployable services communicating over the network, each owning its data.
A web server serves static content and proxies requests; an application server executes the application code.
A defined contract by which one piece of software calls another, hiding the implementation behind it.
An architectural style using HTTP methods and URLs to act on resources, typically exchanging JSON.
GET reads, POST creates, PUT and PATCH update, DELETE removes; 2xx succeeded, 4xx the client erred, 5xx the server erred.
topics.notes: The 4xx-versus-5xx distinction locates fault and is commonly tested.

topics.description: Structured text formats for exchanging data between systems, JSON being the current default for web APIs.
A buffer decoupling producers from consumers so components need not be available simultaneously.
Data in tables with defined schema and relationships, queried with SQL and offering transactional guarantees.
Non-relational stores — document, key-value, column, graph — trading strict schema and joins for scale and flexibility.
topics.notes: A named comparison; choosing between them for a scenario is likely.

topics.description: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, and JOIN — enough to read a query and understand what it does.
The structure of the data, the relation holding rows, and the structure that makes lookups fast at the cost of write speed and space.
Atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability — the guarantees that make a transaction all-or-nothing and durable.
Holding frequently used results in fast storage, accepting staleness in exchange for speed.
Whether a server retains client state between requests, which determines how easily instances can be added or replaced.
What the system must do — the behaviours and features users can observe.
How well it must do it: performance, availability, security, usability, maintainability. Often decisive for architecture.
topics.notes: A named comparison; classifying a given requirement is a likely question.

topics.description: Drawing out real needs through interviews, workshops, observation and document study, since stated wants and actual needs differ.
A description of how an actor interacts with the system to achieve a goal, including alternate paths.
Diagramming the current or intended workflow so inefficiencies and hand-offs become visible.
Comparing current state to desired state and defining the work that closes the difference.
Assessing whether a proposal is technically, operationally and economically achievable before committing.
Ordering requirements by value and necessity, MoSCoW being a common scheme.
Linking each requirement to its design, implementation and test, so coverage can be demonstrated.
Verification asks whether it was built right; validation asks whether the right thing was built.
topics.notes: A named comparison and easy to invert.

topics.description: Testing by the people who will use the system, against their real needs rather than the specification alone.
Writing requirements down unambiguously so they can be agreed, built against, and tested.
Software distributed with source code and the rights to use, study, modify and redistribute it.
The Free Software Foundation’s framing emphasising user freedom rather than development method. Free as in freedom, not price.
topics.notes: The free-as-in-speech distinction is frequently tested.

path: Open Source Initiative and the Open Source Definition
topics.description: The body and criteria determining whether a licence genuinely qualifies as open source.
Software distributed without source or redistribution rights, licensed under terms set by the vendor.
Human-readable code versus compiled machine code. Some licences require source to accompany distributed binaries.
MIT, Apache 2.0 and BSD allow reuse in proprietary products, typically requiring only attribution.
topics.notes: Permissive versus copyleft is the central comparison in this competency.

topics.description: GPL and similar require derivative works distributed to others to be released under the same terms, which is why copyleft is called viral.
The strong copyleft licence used by the Linux kernel (v2), requiring source availability for distributed derivatives.
A weaker copyleft permitting linking from proprietary software without imposing the licence on the whole work.
Extends copyleft to software offered over a network, closing the gap where a service is used but never distributed.
Short permissive licences requiring little more than preservation of the copyright notice.
A permissive licence that additionally grants patent rights and requires notice of modifications.
Licences for content rather than code, and the status of work with no reserved rights.
Whether differently-licensed components may lawfully be combined; permissive code can generally enter copyleft projects but not the reverse.
topics.notes: The asymmetry is the point and is commonly examined.

topics.description: Meeting obligations for attribution, notice, and source availability when distributing software built on open source.
Offering the same software under both an open source and a commercial licence.
An agreement clarifying the rights a contributor grants to a project.
An inventory of components and their licences, increasingly required for supply-chain transparency.
Users, contributors, committers and maintainers, with responsibility increasing along the chain.
Issues, pull requests, code review and codes of conduct as the normal contribution path.
Taking a copy in a new independent direction, a right open source licences explicitly protect.
Neutral bodies such as the Linux Foundation and Apache Software Foundation holding assets and setting governance so no single vendor controls a project.
